summary: Extends RSVP-TE to bind two point-to-point unidirectional label switched paths into one associated bidirectional path. It defines new Association Types for the ASSOCIATION and Extended ASSOCIATION objects, supporting two-way traffic where each direction may follow a different route.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP-TE sets up traffic engineering paths one direction at a time, so a service that needs to work in both directions ends up with two separate paths. This RFC defines the messages that bind those two paths together, and adds a way for one end to ask the other end to create its half of the pair.

questions: what is an associated bidirectional lsp
what is single-sided provisioning in rsvp-te
subtitle: How RSVP-TE ties two one-way label switched paths into a single two-way path, with independent or one-sided setup.

tldr.problem: Traffic engineering needs a two-way path, but RSVP-TE can only signal one direction at a time. The two halves have to be bound together so that each end knows which path is the partner of its own, and so that the pair can be provisioned and protected as one service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two new Association Types for the ASSOCIATION and Extended ASSOCIATION objects, one for double-sided provisioning and one for single-sided, and adds a new REVERSE_LSP object that lets the initiating node trigger and parameter the reverse path from the far end.
tldr.outcome: The result is an associated bidirectional label switched path in which the two directions may follow different routes and may reserve different bandwidths. RFC 7551 is a Proposed Standard, published in May 2015, and it was later updated by RFC 8537.

today: RFC 7551 is a Proposed Standard, published in May 2015, and it was later updated by RFC 8537. It has not been obsoleted, and the RFC text does not describe any deployments.

sections.title: Why Bind Two Paths Together
sections.content:
The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) requirements document RFC 5654 specifies that MPLS-TP MUST support associated bidirectional point-to-point label switched paths (LSPs). The RFC quotes the requirements it repeats: the end points of an associated bidirectional LSP MUST be aware of the pairing relationship of the forward and reverse LSPs used to support the bidirectional service, and nodes where both the forward and backward directions transit the same node in the same layer SHOULD be aware of that pairing as well. The same requirements are repeated in RFC 6373.

An associated bidirectional LSP is also useful for protection switching for Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM) messages that require a return path. A variety of applications exist with different upstream and downstream bandwidth requirements, and RFC 5654 requires MPLS-TP to support bidirectional LSPs with asymmetric bandwidth, meaning the amount of reserved bandwidth differs between the forward and backward directions. The approach for supporting asymmetric bandwidth co-routed bidirectional LSPs is defined in RFC 6387.

The method of association and the corresponding RSVP ASSOCIATION object are defined in RFC 4872, RFC 4873 and RFC 6689, where the object is used to associate a recovery LSP with the LSP it protects. The object also has broader applicability as a mechanism to associate RSVP states, and RFC 6780 defines the Extended ASSOCIATION objects that can be applied more generally. This RFC uses the term "(Extended) ASSOCIATION Objects" to refer to both families.

Section 2.2 gives the one definition the document needs. Two reverse unidirectional LSPs are set up in the opposite directions between a pair of source and destination nodes to form an associated bidirectional LSP. A reverse unidirectional LSP originates on the same node where the forward unidirectional LSP terminates, and it terminates on the same node where the forward unidirectional LSP originates.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic engineering paths run one way at a time. When a service needs both ways, the two one-way paths are bound into a pair so that each end can recognise its partner and so that the pair can be managed as one thing.

sections.title: Single-Sided and Double-Sided Provisioning
sections.content:
The forward and reverse unidirectional LSPs of an associated bidirectional LSP are established, monitored and protected independently, as specified by RFC 5654. Configuration information about them can be provided at one or both endpoints, and that choice gives two models.

In single-sided provisioning, the Traffic Engineering (TE) tunnel is configured only on one endpoint. An LSP for this tunnel is initiated by the initiating endpoint with the (Extended) ASSOCIATION and REVERSE_LSP objects inserted in the Path message. The other endpoint then creates the corresponding reverse TE tunnel and signals the reverse LSP in response, using the information from the REVERSE_LSP object and the other objects present in the received Path message. One endpoint does the work of describing the pair; the other follows it.

In double-sided provisioning, two unidirectional TE tunnels are configured independently, one on each endpoint. The LSPs for the tunnels are signaled with (Extended) ASSOCIATION objects inserted in the Path message by both endpoints, so that the two LSPs are to be associated to form a bidirectional LSP. Neither end waits for the other: both signal, and the association is recognised from the objects they carry.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to set the pair up. Either one end describes both halves and the far end builds its half from that description, or each end builds its own half and they are matched afterwards.

sections.title: Three Scenarios and Asymmetric Bandwidth
sections.content:
Section 3.2 lists three scenarios for binding two unidirectional LSPs together into an associated bidirectional LSP: neither unidirectional LSP exists and both must be established; both exist but the association must be established; and one exists but the reverse associated LSP must be established.

The worked example uses the topology of Figure 1, where LSP1 runs from node A to B along the path A, D, B, and LSP2 runs from node B to A along the path B, D, C, A. Once established and associated, the two form an associated bidirectional LSP between nodes A and B. Path Computation Element (PCE) based approaches, described in RFC 4655, may be used for path computation of an associated bidirectional LSP, but those approaches are outside the scope of this document.

In the single-sided provisioning model, creation of the reverse LSP is triggered by the other one. When creation of reverse LSP2 is triggered by LSP1, LSP1 is provisioned first, or refreshed if it already exists, at node A. LSP1 is then signaled with an (Extended) ASSOCIATION and REVERSE_LSP object in the Path message, and the Association Type indicates single-sided provisioning. On receiving that Path message, node B establishes reverse LSP2, and the (Extended) ASSOCIATION object inserted in LSP2's Path message is the same as the one received in LSP1's Path message. In the double-sided provisioning model, both LSPs are signaled independently with (Extended) ASSOCIATION objects whose Association Type indicates double-sided provisioning, and the two are bound together on the basis of identical (Extended) ASSOCIATION objects in their Path messages. In all three scenarios the LSPs to be selected for the association are provisioned by the management action applied at both endpoints.

Section 3.3 covers bandwidth. The REVERSE_LSP object allows the initiating node of a single-sided provisioned LSP to trigger creation of the reverse LSP on the remote node, and a SENDER_TSPEC object can be added as a subobject to specify a different bandwidth for the reverse LSP. Adding the object also lets the initiating node control other aspects of the reverse LSP, such as its path, by including other objects in it. In the double-sided model the two unidirectional LSPs are simply established with separate bandwidths, which may or may not be identical, and the association is still based purely on the identical contents of their (Extended) ASSOCIATION objects.

Section 3.4 adds recovery. Recovery of each unidirectional LSP forming the bidirectional LSP is independent and is based on the parameters signaled in their respective RSVP Path messages. Recovery LSP association is based on the identical content of the (Extended) ASSOCIATION objects signaled in their Path messages during the initial LSP setup, for both single-sided and double-sided provisioning. Multiple ASSOCIATION objects may be present in the signaling of a single LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: The pair can be built in three situations: neither half exists, both halves exist, or one half exists. The two halves may reserve different amounts of bandwidth, and each half recovers on its own, so a fault in one direction does not necessarily tear the other down.

sections.title: The ASSOCIATION Object and Its New Types
sections.content:
The (Extended) ASSOCIATION object is what binds the two paths together, and this RFC adds two new values for its Association Type field. Value 3 is Double-Sided Associated Bidirectional LSP (D) and value 4 is Single-Sided Associated Bidirectional LSP (A). To bind two reverse unidirectional LSPs into an associated bidirectional LSP, the Association Type MUST be set to indicate either single-sided or double-sided LSPs.

Two more fields matter. For both single-sided and double-sided provisioning, the Association ID MUST be set to a value assigned by the node that originates the association for the bidirectional LSP. The Association Source MUST be set to an address selected by that same node, which may for example be a management entity or, in the case of single-sided provisioning, an address assigned to the node that originates the LSP.

The Extended ASSOCIATION object carries the same three values, and the RFC adds two of its own. Global Association Source, when used, MUST be set to the Global_ID of the node that originates the association, as defined in RFC 6370. Extended Association ID, when used, MUST be set to a value selected by the node that originates the association.

Section 4.1 shows where the objects travel. The Path message format gains two optional entries, [ <ASSOCIATION> ... ] and [ <REVERSE_LSP> ... ], inserted after <ADMIN_STATUS> and before <POLICY_DATA>. The document uses the Routing Backus-Naur Form (RBNF) to define message formats, as defined in RFC 5511.
sections.plainLanguage: The binding is carried in an object that travels with the path setup request. Two new values of its type field say whether one end or both ends are in charge, and two other fields say who is in charge and which pair of paths is meant.

sections.title: The REVERSE_LSP Object
sections.content:
The REVERSE_LSP object is carried in the Path message of a forward LSP to provide information to be used by the reverse LSP. It also indicates that the LSP is the forward LSP of a single-sided associated bidirectional LSP. Its class number is 203 and its class type is 1, and the object itself is a sequence of subobjects.

The subobjects are used to override the default contents of the Path message of a reverse LSP. They are zero or more variable-length subobjects that have the same format as RSVP objects, and any object that may be carried in a Path message may be carried in the REVERSE_LSP object. Subobject ordering MUST follow any Path message object ordering requirements. The RFC lists examples of the Path message objects that can be carried this way: the SENDER_TSPEC object, the EXPLICIT_ROUTE object (ERO), the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object, the ADMIN_STATUS object, the LSP_REQUIRED_ATTRIBUTES object and the PROTECTION object.
sections.plainLanguage: This object is the instruction sheet sent to the far end: it says what the reverse path should look like, and it can carry the bandwidth, the route and the protection settings for that path.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
The rules for the (Extended) ASSOCIATION object are those of RFC 4872 and RFC 6780, with additions. The association of bidirectional LSPs is always upstream initiated, so the new Association Types are only to be interpreted in Path messages; they SHOULD NOT be used in ASSOCIATION objects carried in Resv messages and SHOULD be ignored if present there.

An ingress node MUST insert an (Extended) ASSOCIATION object into the Path message of the unidirectional LSP that is part of the associated bidirectional LSP it initiates. If either Global Association Source or Extended Association Address is required, an Extended ASSOCIATION object MUST be inserted; otherwise an ASSOCIATION object MAY be used. Objects with both single-sided and double-sided Association Types MUST NOT be added or sent in the same Path message. The ingress node MUST set the Association Type field to "Single-Sided Associated Bidirectional LSP" when single-sided provisioning is used, and to "Double-Sided Associated Bidirectional LSP" when double-sided provisioning is used. A transit node MAY identify the unidirectional LSPs of the pair from the objects carried in Path messages. When an egress node receives a Path message containing one of these Association Types, it MUST attempt to identify the other LSPs with which the one being processed is associated, and an LSP that is not associated at the time of signaling, for example during rerouting or re-optimization, is not necessarily an error condition.

Teardown follows the standard procedures of RFC 3209 and RFC 3473, with or without the administrative status. The teardown procedures of the two unidirectional LSPs are independent of each other, so one LSP may follow a graceful teardown with administrative status while the reverse is torn down without it. When an LSP signaled with one of these Association Types is torn down, the processing node SHALL remove the binding of that LSP to any previously identified associated bidirectional LSP.

The rules for the REVERSE_LSP object are stricter. When a node initiates setup of an LSP using a Path message containing an ASSOCIATION or Extended ASSOCIATION object whose Association Type is "Single-Sided Associated Bidirectional LSP", the Path message MUST carry the REVERSE_LSP object to trigger creation of a reverse LSP on the egress node. A transit node receiving a valid Path message containing a REVERSE_LSP object MUST forward it unchanged in the outgoing Path message. An egress node receiving a Path message with a REVERSE_LSP object MUST verify that the message also contains an ASSOCIATION or Extended ASSOCIATION object with the single-sided Association Type; if it does not, the Path message MUST NOT trigger a reverse LSP, and the failure SHOULD NOT trigger any RSVP message but can be logged locally.

Once validated, the egress node MUST create an LSP in the reverse direction or reject the Path message. If the creation of a reverse LSP fails, the egress node MUST return a PathErr with Error Code "Admission Control Failure" (1) and the Sub-code "Reverse LSP Failure" (6) that this document defines. The egress node MUST use the subobjects contained in the REVERSE_LSP object to initiate the reverse LSP. Where a subobject is not present, the egress node SHOULD build the reverse Path message from the received forward Path message: it SHOULD copy the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE, CLASS_TYPE, LABEL_REQUEST, ASSOCIATION, ADMIN_STATUS and PROTECTION objects; it SHOULD set the IP address in the reverse LSP's SESSION object to the address carried in the received SENDER_TEMPLATE object and conversely; and it SHOULD include a received RECORD_ROUTE object in the reverse Path message. There are no specific requirements for other objects.

Two rules protect the consistency of the pair over time. The contents of a forward LSP may change over its life, and such changes MUST result in corresponding changes in the reverse LSP; in particular any object or subobject copied when the reverse LSP was created MUST be copied when it is modified in the forward LSP, and a trigger Path message MUST be processed. And when the egress node receives a PathTear message for the forward LSP, it MUST remove the associated reverse LSP using standard PathTear processing. Removal of the REVERSE_LSP object from the received Path message SHOULD cause the egress node to tear down any previously established reverse LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules are mostly about who does what. The starting node must mark the request; the far end must check that the request is legitimate before it builds the other half; and every later change to one half has to be copied to the other.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Three registry entries are added. The "Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) Signaling Parameters" registry holds an "Association Type" subregistry, which gains value 3 for Double-Sided Associated Bidirectional LSP (D) and value 4 for Single-Sided Associated Bidirectional LSP (A).

The "Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) Parameters" registry holds the "Class Names, Class Numbers, and Class Types" subregistry, which gains Class Number 203 for the REVERSE_LSP object with Class Type or C-type equal to 1, in the 11bbbbbb range.

The same RSVP Parameters registry holds the "Error Codes and Globally-Defined Error Value Sub-Codes" subregistry, which gains the Sub-code "Reverse LSP Failure" with the value 6 under Error Code 01, "Admission Control Failure".
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the lists of numbers that make these messages work. This RFC adds two association types, one new object number for the reverse-path instruction, and one new error code for when the far end cannot build the other half.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The two new Association Types introduce, by themselves, no additional information to the signaling, and the related security considerations are already covered in RFC 6780.

The REVERSE_LSP object is carried in the Path message of a forward LSP of a single-sided associated bidirectional LSP, and it can carry parameters for the reverse LSP. That does allow more information to be conveyed, but it is not fundamentally different from the information that is already carried in a bidirectional LSP message. The processing of such messages is already subject to local policy as well as to the security considerations discussed in the MPLS and GMPLS security framework, RFC 5920.
sections.plainLanguage: The new objects do not carry anything the signalling does not already carry, so they do not need their own security rules. The rules that apply to the surrounding framework still apply.
